title: Could Democrats' Midterm Victories Finally Spell the End of the Electoral College?
snippet: Following major statehouse gains in key battleground states, Democrats are laying the groundwork for a historic push to bypass the Electoral College in time for the 2028 presidential race.
content:
WASHINGTON — A quiet legislative movement in state capitals across the country could fundamentally alter how Americans choose their commander-in-chief by 2028.

Following recent midterm victories, Democrats gained total control of state governments—holding the governor's mansion and majorities in both legislative chambers—across five critical battlegrounds: Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona. Now, progressive state lawmakers are preparing to leverage those new trifectas to advance an ambitious proposal that would effectively bypass the traditional Electoral College.

The 270 Threshold Within Reach

The plan centers on the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC), an agreement launched in 2006. Member states pledge to award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential ticket wins the overall popular vote nationwide, regardless of the individual state's local outcome.

To date, 18 states and Washington, D.C., have signed the compact into law. Together, they command 222 electoral votes—short of the 270 needed to trigger the agreement. However, if the five newly flipped battleground states sign on, their collective 61 electoral votes would push the compact's tally to 283, officially activating the initiative for future presidential contests.

State lawmakers in key capitals have already expressed plans to prioritize the effort during upcoming legislative sessions, fueled by the expanded statehouse majorities.

A Polarizing Modern Reform

Frustration with the Electoral College has mounted among Democrats over the last two decades, particularly after George W. Bush in 2000 and Donald Trump in 2016 secured the White House despite losing the nationwide popular vote. Supporters contend that shifting to a national popular vote model would compel presidential campaigns to cater to voters everywhere, rather than concentrating almost exclusively on a handful of purple swing states.

Republicans, however, largely oppose the reform. Opponents argue the compact undermines the constitutional framework designed by the Founders to ensure smaller states maintain a voice in national governance. When Virginia enacted the compact after Democrats gained full government control there, conservative leaders denounced the measure as an unconstitutional attempt to disenfranchise local voters.

Formidable Challenges Ahead

Despite political momentum, key obstacles remain. Lawmakers face pressure to focus on immediate economic concerns like inflation and local spending rather than procedural election reforms. Furthermore, internal Democratic dissent has stalled past efforts; Nevada's former Democratic governor vetoed a popular vote bill in 2019 over fears it would strip the silver state of its outsized presidential influence.

Should the compact reach the 270-vote threshold, it will also face immediate legal resistance. Legal scholars note that the U.S. Constitution's Compact Clause restricts states from entering into interstate agreements without explicit congressional approval—a hurdle that would almost certainly trigger a high-stakes showdown before the Supreme Court.
